Undergraduate women (N = 143) completed self-reports on exercise behavior, body orientation, body appreciation, and body-related talk. Results showed that conversations about weight loss/dieting and conversations about exercise differentially predicted body appreciation. Importantly, multiple regression analyses showed that the relationship between talk type and body appreciation was explained by the object– process dichotomy: Conversations about exercise oriented women to consider what their bodies can do which, in turn, predicted appreciation of one's body. In contrast, the relationship between conversations about weight loss/dieting and body appreciation was mediated by negative attitudes about one's body but not by an object orientation.

Research suggests that young women in Western industrialized nations are concerned with their appearance, and some researchers identify the media (e.g. Gonzalez et al., 2013; Groesz et al., 2002; cf. Ferguson et al., 2011), parents (e.g. Stice et al., 1999; Unikel et al., 2013), and peers (e.g. Clark and Tiggemann, 2006) as three social influences that contribute to the development of body image concerns (Thompson et al., 1999). However, research has disproportionately addressed how and when the media promotes undesirable physical selfevaluations. Consequently, in the present study, we focus on the role of peers and specifically target body talk to examine whether different types of body talk between friends might differentially predict how women feel about their
bodies, and whether the relationships could be explained by the object–process dichotomy.

Sociocultural models of body image (e.g. Smolak and Levine, 2001; Thompson et al., 1999) posit that family and peers influence how girls evaluate their physical selves through communication of the value of appearance. For

example, Unikel et al. (2013) found that family's criticism of weight/shape of young women predicted disordered eating behaviors, in part, because criticism contributed to young women's internalization of the thin ideal. Among peers, messages may communicate the need to fit the ideal body image and may serve to solidify friendships and validate the self. Indeed, Nichter and Vuckovic (1994) coined the term "fat talk" to describe conversations about appearance, dieting, and the need to lose weight, and Nichter (2002) demonstrated that such conversations helped to maintain friendships.

Relevant to the current study is the work by Stice et al. (2003) that demonstrated that young women were more dissatisfied with their own bodies when exposed to a slim female confederate who talked about how fat she felt, compared to participants exposed to a slim female confederate who talked about a neutral topic. The impact of fat talk is also implied in the work by Ousley et al., (2008) in which they found that fat talk was prevalent among undergraduate students, and particularly among those with eating pathology; this is of interest because conversations likely reflect what is of relevance. Given that young women are concerned about weight and shape (Striegel-Moore and Franko, 2002), it is not surprising that undergraduates talk about ideal bodies, and how they, or others, strive toward (or fail to achieve) those ideals. Other research demonstrates that the frequency of fat talk is associated with depression, perceived pressure to be thin (Arroyo and Harwood, 2012), more body dissatisfaction, and internalization of the thin ideal (e.g. Salk and Engeln-Maddox, 2011). Internalization of the thin ideal is central to understanding women's body image concerns (e.g. Ahern et al., 2011; Mask and Blanchard, 2011), and fat talk may be one mechanism by which women adopt the cultural ideal as a standard.

Whereas it seems that conversations about weight loss and dieting contribute to women's preoccupation with weight and/or shape, the effect of conversations about exercise is less clear. Some research suggests that women who

talk about exercise are still engaging in "fat talk." For example, to assess fat talk, Ousley et al. (2008) included five topics: (1) ideal eating and exercise habits, (2) fears of becoming out-of-shape or overweight, (3) eating and exercise habits compared to others, (4) other people's shape and appearance, and (5) supplements, meal replacements, and muscle building strategies. Arroyo and Harwood (2012) assessed fat talk using similar questions, and although they documented the consequences of engaging in such conversations, the merging of food-related and exercise-related topics suggests that the effect of each is similar. Yet it seems reasonable to consider that food-related talk and exercise-related talk differentially impact self-views, because the effects of actually engaging in dieting and exercise are not necessarily similar.

Food/diet and exercise are both means to lose weight and may represent attempts to achieve an ideal body. Indeed, excessive exercise is considered to be a symptom of eating disorders just as restrictive eating is (American Psychiatric Association, 2000), and in that way, exercise is similar to dieting. However, research suggests that there may be benefits of engaging in exercise for body image (for a review, see Martin and Lichtenberger, 2002). For example, regular aerobic exercise was associated with lessened physique anxiety among female college students (Bartlewski et al., 1996), and Martin Ginis et al. (2005) found that body image for both men and women improved following a 12-week strength training program. More recently, in a meta-analysis of the effects of exercise, Campbell and Hausenblas (2009) concluded that exercise contributes to improvements in body image, and mode of exercise did not moderate the effect. In contrast, food restriction (dieting) is generally viewed as having more negative versus positive physical and psychological consequences (e.g. Polivy, 1998). If engaging in dieting and exercise can predict opposing effects, it seems plausible that conversations related to these topics also differ in terms of their effects.

Indeed, Wasylkiw and Williamson (2013) noted that in a sample of undergraduate students, increased talk about exercise predicted less reported dissatisfaction with one's appearance, whereas increased talk about food and weight loss predicted increased dissatisfaction. Wasylkiw and Williamson proposed that the topics subsumed by the broader category of body talk orients those involved to think about their bodies in terms of object or process.

When Franzoi (1995) introduced the object– process dichotomy in his analysis of gender differences in body esteem, he argued that women were more likely to focus their attention on how their bodies looked (body-asobject), whereas men were more likely to focus their attention on how their bodies functioned (body-as-process), likely because of gender roles. Franzoi also provided evidence that both undergraduate men and women tended to hold less favorable attitudes toward the body-as-object than the body-as-process. For women, there is evidence that appearance evaluations tend to be negative. Along with theoretical discourse (e.g. Fredrickson and Roberts, 1997), empirical research supports the idea that objectifying the female body is consequential. Specifically, for women, the tendency to view the body-as-object is linked to body dissatisfaction (e.g. Franzoi, 1995), depression (e.g. Stice and Bearman, 2001), internalization of thin ideal (e.g. Morry and Staska, 2001), restrained eating, and eating disorders (e.g. Dohnt and Tiggemann, 2006). Much less research has examined the impact of thinking about the body-as-process.

Although, as noted earlier, exercise may positively impact evaluations of the physical self, few studies have examined the direct impact of viewing the body-as-process versus viewing the body-as-object. Certainly, there is evidence that men tend to hold positive views of their physical selves more than women do

(e.g. Van den Berg et al., 2007), and men are more likely to place greater value on their physical competencies compared to women (e.g. Calogero, 2009). Additionally, athletes hold more positive views of their physical selves in comparison to nonathletes (e.g. Hausenblas and Downs, 2001). Moreover, among young adolescent boys, Farquhar and Wasylkiw (2007) showed that media ideals emphasizing appearance led to increased body dissatisfaction, whereas media ideals emphasizing process led to lessened dissatisfaction. Thus, there seems to be some support that viewing the body-asprocess is beneficial for body image. Indeed, Franzoi (1995) suggested that one way to alter views about physical appearance would be to engage in athletic activities because such activity would orient women to thinking about their bodies as process.

Overall, the research reviewed suggests that "fat talk" and the object–process dichotomy contribute to women's body image. Importantly, the research also appears to support our contention that topics typically covered under the rubric of "fat talk" may actually differentially impact body image. Thus, we propose that the mechanism by which conversations about diet and exercise impact women's self-perceptions is rooted in the object–process dichotomy.

In the present study, we had three goals. First, we expected that women would endorse higher scores on the body-as-object orientation versus body-as-process, and that engagement in exercise would correspond to increases in body-asprocess orientation and body appreciation. Second, we expected that weight loss talk would negatively predict and exercise talk would positively predict body appreciation. Third, we hypothesized that viewing the bodyas-object would mediate the relationship between weight loss talk and body appreciation, and viewing the body-as-process would mediate the relationship between exercise talk and body appreciation.

A convenience sample of 143 undergraduate women was recruited from an Introductory Psychology class to participate in the present study in return for course credit. Based on previous research, this sample size was judged to be adequate to test the hypotheses. To maintain a homogenous sample, we eliminated data from one participant with a reported age of 46 years. Of the remaining 142 participants, ages ranged between 17 and 24 years (M = 18.68 years; standard deviation (SD) = 1.05 years). Of the 130 participants who indicated ethnicity, 86.9 percent (n = 113) specified being Caucasian, and of the 135 participants who responded to 1 item about year of study, 71.1 percent (n = 96) specified that they were in their first year of study.

Despite the potential for biased responses, we assessed body mass index (BMI) from selfreported weight and height (in kg/m2) because BMI was not the primary variable of interest, but we wanted to include it as a control variable in our analyses involving the relationship between conversation and body image. Of the 138 participants who reported body weight, 8.7 percent (n = 12) were underweight (15–18.5 kg/ m2), 77.5 percent (n = 107) were normal (18.5– 24.9 kg/m2), 10.87 percent (n = 15) were overweight (25–29.9 kg/m2), and 6.71 percent (n = 4) were obese (>30 kg/m2); the mean BMI was 22.22 (SD = 3.46).

Exercise behavior. Two items were taken from the 7-item Exercise Behaviour Survey (Melbye, 2005) to gauge the activity level of participants. The first item assessed frequency of physical exercise with responses ranging from 1 (0 times) to 4 (5 or more times), and the second item assessed length of each exercise session with responses ranging from 1 (0–15 minutes) to 5 (60 minutes or more). The 2 items were summed to yield a possible range from 2 to 9 with higher scores indicating engagement in
more exercise. In the present study, Cronbach's alpha for the 2 items was .67.

Body orientation. The Body Esteem Scale (BES; Franzoi and Shields, 1984) was used to assess the attitudes toward body functioning and attitudes toward body appearance. Participants indicated their attitudes to 35 items (e.g. "waist," "physical condition") on a scale from 1 (strongly negative) to 5 (strongly positive). Twelve items represent body-as-process, and responses were summed to yield a possible range of 12 to 60. Seventeen items represent body-as-object, and responses were summed to yield a possible range of 17 to 85. Higher scores on each subscale indicate that the participant has more positive attitudes toward either appearance or functionality. In the present study, Cronbach's alphas were .80 and .88 for body-as-object and body-as-process, respectively.

Whereas the BES assesses attitudes toward appearance and functioning, we were also interested in assessing participants' focus, and propose that people likely differ in the extent to which they regard their physical selves in terms of appearance and functionality independent of their evaluations of those aspects. Thus, one item was used to assess an orientation toward process ("I think about my body in terms of what it can do") and one item was used to assess an orientation toward appearance ("I think about my body in terms of how attractive it is"). Participants responded to both items on a scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

Body image. To assess how women felt about their physical selves, we used Avalos et al.'s (2005) Body Appreciation Scale. Participants rate each of the 13 items on a scale from 1 (never) to 5 (always). Responses were averaged such that the scores can range from 1 to 5, with higher scores indicating a positive attitude toward one's physical self. Cronbach's alpha in the present study was .92.

For the 6 items assessing exercise talk (e.g. "How often do you talk about going to the gym?"), participants responded on a scale from 1 (very rarely) to 5 (almost always). Responses were summed to yield a total score that could range from 6 to 30, with higher scores indicating more exercise talk. In the present sample, Cronbach's alpha was .72. Responses to 3 items (e.g. "How often do you talk about weight loss?") were summed to yield an index of conversation frequency about weight loss and dieting. The possible range for this subscale was 3 to 15, with higher scores indicating more frequent talk. Cronbach's alpha for weight-loss- or diet-related talk was .84, indicating adequate internal consistency reliability. The items used to assess body-related talk are presented in the Appendix 1.

Descriptive statistics and bivariate correlations among measures are presented in Table 1. As expected, participants were significantly more likely to be oriented toward appearance versus performance, t(140) = 4.06, p < .001, r = .33, 95 percent confidence interval (CI): (.17, .47). Additionally, we averaged subscale scores on the BES, and a paired t-test did showed that women's attitudes toward body-as-process (M

= 3.30, SD = .74) were more positive than those toward body-as-object (M = 3.16, SD = .55), t(141) = 3.34, p < .001, r = .26, 95 percent CI: (.10, .41). The correlations in Table 1 for exercise show that exercise was strongly positively related to body appreciation and with a process orientation, whereas it was negatively associated with an object orientation.

With respect to conversations, the pattern of results shown in Table 1 indicates that the relationships between body esteem, body orientation, body appreciation, and body-related talk are as expected. Additionally, the pattern of results indicates that the relationships between body esteem, body orientation, body appreciation, and body-related talk are as expected; more positive views about one's body functioning and one's body appearance related to increased body appreciation. Moreover, body appreciation was positively related to an orientation toward performance but negatively related to appearance orientation. Similarly, conversations about exercise were positively associated with body appreciation, whereas conversations about weight loss and dieting were negatively associated with body appreciation.
To test the hypothesis that weight loss talk would negatively predict body appreciation and

exercise talk would positively predict, a simultaneous multiple regression analysis was specified. In this analysis, we included BMI as a control variable because previous research shows that relative body mass is a robust predictor of body image. Owing to missing responses, the results are based on 138 participants. The overall model was significant and accounted for 28 percent of the variance in body appreciation, F(3, 134) = 17.20, p < .001. Consistent with previous research, increased BMI was associated with less appreciation of one's body when controlling for body-related talk, variance inflation factor (VIF) = 1.02, B = −.07, standard error (SE) = .02, β = −.32, 95 percent CI: (−.47, −.17), p < .01. Moreover, as hypothesized, increased talk about weight loss and dieting predicted less appreciation of one's body, VIF = 1.08, B = −.07, SE = .01, β = −.37, 95 percent CI: (−.53, −.21), p < .01, whereas increased talk about exercise predicted more appreciation of one's body, VIF = 1.07, B = .03, SE = .01, β = .23, 95 percent CI: (.07, .39), p < .01. All variables included in the model were normally distributed, and as indicated by the VIF values, multicollinearity was not an issue in this analysis (see Myers, 1990; Tabachnick and Fidell, 2013).

Mediation analyses were performed using Preacher and Hayes' (2008) procedure to test the hypothesis that body esteem (i.e. attitudes toward body performance, attitudes toward appearance) and body orientation (i.e. body-asprocess, body-as-object) mediated the relationship between body-related talk (i.e. exercise talk, weight loss talk) and body appreciation. In these analyses, mediation is significant if the 95 percent bias-corrected and accelerated CIs for the indirect effect do not include 0.
In Figure 1(a), the relationship between exercise-related talk and body appreciation is shown. Results, based on 5000 bootstrapped

samples, indicated that although the total effect of exercise talk on body appreciation was significant, the direct effect was not. Thus, the relationship between exercise talk and body appreciation was fully mediated by body esteem. Moreover, the bias-corrected and accelerated 95 percent CI of .01 to .04 for attitudes toward performance and the 95 percent CI of .01 to .03 for attitudes toward appearance suggest that both types of body esteem mediated the relationship. Thus, participants who indicated high frequencies of exercise-related talk were more likely to appreciate their bodies because they held positive views of their bodies' performance and appearance.

As can be seen in Figure 1(b), results, based on 5000 bootstrapped samples, indicated that the total effect of exercise talk on body appreciation was significant but that the direct effect was not. The bias-corrected and accelerated 95 percent CI of .01 to .02 for performance orientation and the 95 percent CI of −.004 to .01 for appearance orientation suggest that only performance orientation fully mediated the relationship. Thus, participants who indicated high frequencies of exercise-related talk were more likely to appreciate their bodies because they were more likely to hold a process orientation.

In Figure 1(c), the results of the same analysis for the proposed mediational model involving weight-loss/diet talk and body appreciation are presented. Results, based on 5000 bootstrapped samples, indicated that the direct effect of weight-loss/diet talk was significant, suggesting that body attitudes partially mediated the relationship. The bias-corrected and accelerated 95 percent CI of −.02 to .00 for attitudes toward performance and the 95 percent CI of −.04 to −.01 for attitudes toward appearance suggest that only attitudes toward appearance partially mediated the relationship. Thus, participants who engaged in talk about weight loss and dieting were less appreciative of their bodies because they held more negative attitudes about appearance.

As can be seen in Figure 1(d), the results are based on 5000 bootstrapped samples and demonstrate that neither performance nor appearance orientation mediated the relationship between weight-loss/diet talk and body appreciation. That is, the bias-corrected and

accelerated 95 percent CI was −.01 to .01 for performance orientation and −.02 to .001 for appearance orientation. Thus, there are likely mediating processes between talk about weight loss/dieting and body appreciation not considered in this study.

The present study was undertaken to examine whether conversations about weight loss/dieting and exercise differentially predicted body appreciation. Key to our study was the proposed mediational model whereby we examined whether the object–process dichotomy was responsible for the relationships between conversation topic and body image.

Our results supported our hypotheses, and three findings are noteworthy. First, we began by showing that our sample of undergraduate women endorsed a stronger body-as-object orientation than they did a body-as-process orientation. These results are in line with the literature documenting self-objectification among women. Additionally, we showed that frequency of exercise was positively related to a process orientation, supporting Franzoi's (1995) assertion that exercise may be one way to alter women's orientation.

Second, according to our sample, conversations about weight loss and dieting and conversations about exercise differentially predict body appreciation. The finding that, when controlling for body mass, talk about exercise predicted increased appreciation of one's body whereas talk about weight loss/dieting predicted decreased appreciation highlights the importance of parsing out the topics presumed to comprise fat talk.

Third, our proposed mediational models received support because we showed that the relationship between conversation topics and body image was mediated by body attitudes and body orientation. Women with high frequencies of exercise talk tended to hold positive attitudes toward their bodies, and this relationship was mediated by object–process attitudes and orientation. In other words, women who engage in exercise talk tend to view their bodies positively and adopt a body-as-process orientation that, in turn, contributes to body appreciation. For the relationship between weight-loss/diet talk and body image, our results are less clear. That is, women who spend time talking about

weight loss and dieting tend to view their bodies negatively, and such negative appearance attitudes contributed to decreased appreciation of one's body; however, the relationship between talk and body image was not due to variability in object–process orientations.

Our results are limited in at least three ways. First, our sample is limited in generalizability because it comprised undergraduate women. Although friends are important for undergraduates (e.g. Buote et al., 2007) and comprise a large proportion of their social network (Hays and Oxley, 1986), the role of friends (and their conversations) may be more (or less) critical for other age groups. Additionally, given the lack of research exploring men's body image concerns (Grogan, 2008), the extension of the role of peer conversations among men would be an important contribution to the topics covered here.

Second, improvements and refinements of measures would be beneficial. For example, we used only one index of body image, and although this measure is a psychometrically sound tool (Avalos et al., 2005), it only focuses on the acceptance and appreciation of one's physique, and inclusion of other measures designed to assess other aspects of body image, such as social physique anxiety, internalization of the thin ideal, and body dissatisfaction, would add confidence in our results.

Our assessment of body orientation was also limited. Although Franzoi and Shields (1984) provide a way to divide the BES scale into two subscales reflecting the object–process dichotomy, this scale comprises attitudinal statements. As argued earlier, it seems that individuals might differ in the extent to which they focus on object and/or process and that is likely independent of their attitudes. Thus, we included two single items to assess body orientation. The claim that orientation is not the same as attitudes is supported by the low correlations found between these items and the BES subscale scores. However, although our items were similar to what was done by Franzoi and Shields, these items have not been validated. One might consider choosing a measure from the array of

scales to assess women's self-objectification (see Calogero, 2011 for a review); however, no measure explicitly includes process orientation. Thus, one future direction would be to create a scale that assesses both body orientations, and that is both reliable and valid.

Our assessment of body talk was also limited by the items we used. For example, in asking participants the extent to which they engaged in conversations about exercise, we were not specific. In other words, we did not determine whether the talk focused on actual engagement in exercise and potential positive outcomes or whether the talk was about nonadherence to prescribed standards of exercise. One can imagine that a conversation involving the need to go to the gym or the lack of exercise might affect participants' self-views differently than a conversation about actual engagement in exercise and sport. Additionally, even conversations that appear to reflect body-as-process may highlight appearance concerns. For example, two people may be discussing their feelings of self-consciousness when exercising, which, potentially, could shift one's focus from process to object. Interestingly, there is research that suggests that some athletic activities (e.g. gymnastics, figure skating) do not contribute to positive views of one's physical self, in part, because of the greater emphasis on appearance (e.g. Borgen and Corbin, 1987). Thus, it is likely that the effect of conversations about exercise on women's body image concerns would be moderated by the exact nature of the conversation and future research might consider assessing exercise talk more precisely.

Yet a third limitation to the present study is the causal direction implied by the mediational models. Because data were collected crosssectionally, it is impossible for us to determine the exact causal ordering of the constructs. It may be that being appreciative of one's body leads to focusing on the object–process orientations that, in turn, contribute to women's conversations. Although longitudinal studies might be useful to examine the directionality of the relationships, one could assign participants to
engage in conversations about weight loss or exercise to determine the impact such conversations would have on body orientation and body image.

Whereas the focus of the present study concerned conversations that foster a specific body orientation, future research might uncover additional mechanisms that explain the impact of conversation on women's body image concerns. For example, Ferguson et al. (2011) recently proposed a Catalyst Model of women's body dissatisfaction in which competition among women for mates trigger body dissatisfaction. It is possible that conversations that focus on appearance intensify competition, and in contrast, conversations about exercise reduce competition. This may help to explain why, in the present study, variability in object–process orientations mediated the relationship between exercise talk and body appreciation but not the relationship between weight-loss/diet talk and body appreciation.

Researchers and clinicians alike recognize the importance of peers and friends in the development and maintenance of body image concerns, and conversations are likely one mechanism by which friends exert influence. Young women need to be aware that conversations play a role in their own self-evaluations as that will help them to counteract messages about weight loss and dieting so as to reduce their impact. The findings of the present study suggest that encouraging young women to talk about exercise and physical activity may alter how they view their own bodies. It may be possible to encourage a focus on the functionality of bodies through media such as Health Canada's Participation campaign. Encouraging young women to talk about exercise may begin in classrooms and workshops that include an educational awareness component as well as small group discussions. In summary, viewing one's self in terms of what one can do versus what one looks like may be one means to attain positive body image, and conversations may be one mechanism that promote differing orientations.
